title: Leslie And Ben

jokes.text: Ben's 'deal breaker' threat about Leslie taking his last name, then immediately admitting he was joking
jokes.setup: In the middle of their whirlwind wedding plan, Ben suddenly says he wants Leslie to drop 'Knope' and become 'Leslie Wyatt' — framed as deeply important and symbolic, even escalating to 'Councilwoman Mrs. Ben Wyatt'
jokes.punchline: 'That's fine too. It's a deal breaker.' — then revealed immediately as a tease, 'Sorry, I had to give it a shot.'
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: it subverts the tender romantic scene with a petty demand, the escalation to 'Councilwoman Mrs. Ben Wyatt' is a funny overcorrection, and Ben immediately confessing he was just messing around is perfectly in character — he's playful but never actually controlling. The character integration is high because this joke could only exist between these two specific people and their dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I love you so much. I want to spend the rest of my life with you.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I love you too. Leslie, will you marry me?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yes! Oh my God, yes!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Great. I'm thinking next Saturday.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Next Saturday? Ben, that's six days away.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know. Is that too soon?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: No, it's perfect. I'll call the venue tomorrow.

jokes.text: 'And we just ordered 200 white-chocolate top hats.' / 'We did?' / 'You did, actually. It's under your name.'
jokes.setup: Ben lists reasons they can't get married tonight — they've already reserved a May date
jokes.punchline: The specific absurdity of 200 white-chocolate top hats, followed by Ben having to clarify it was Leslie's solo decision
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '200 white-chocolate top hats' is perfectly Leslie — absurdly elaborate and food-adjacent. The two-beat follow-up where Ben didn't even know about them is a great character joke. Works because it's deeply rooted in who Leslie is.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We don't have a venue, we don't have a cake, we don't have rings, we don't have flowers, we don't have a dress, we don't have officiants—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My parents aren't coming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm just saying, there's a silver lining to all this.

jokes.text: The 'Falcon is entering / Turtledove acknowledges' code names for Ben and Leslie
jokes.setup: Ben calls Leslie on the phone in a normal, urgent situation
jokes.punchline: He announces himself as 'The falcon is entering' and she responds 'The turtledove acknowledges' — treating a simple phone call like a spy operation
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character work — both Leslie and Ben are overachieving nerds who would absolutely assign each other romantic code names for a spontaneous wedding. The specificity of 'turtledove' for Leslie (romantic) and 'falcon' for Ben (aspirationally cool) is charming. The bit plays again later in the episode, giving it running-gag potential.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We've already ordered the white-chocolate top hats for the groomsmen, hired a string quartet that only plays songs in B-flat, and booked a calligrapher to hand-write all 847 place cards.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, white-chocolate top hats? Those are going to melt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's the point, Ben. They're *supposed* to melt. It's a metaphor for the fleeting nature of our wedding day.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Or we could just... not have hats made of food?

jokes.text: Leslie describing her desired look as 'the sensuality of Eleanor Roosevelt combined with the animal magnetism of Lesley Stahl'
jokes.setup: Ann is assigned to handle Leslie's hair, makeup, and dress on short notice
jokes.punchline: Leslie's vision is a hybrid of two non-glamorous political figures known for gravitas rather than sex appeal
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes and is a near-perfect encapsulation of Leslie Knope as a character. Her beauty ideal is two older female journalists/politicians — not actresses, not models — because in Leslie's world, Eleanor Roosevelt IS sexy and Lesley Stahl IS magnetic. The joke works because it's not mocking Leslie; it's celebrating her genuinely unique worldview. The specificity (Lesley Stahl's 'animal magnetism') is hilarious and couldn't be said by any other character. Earns its 8+ rating.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We could do July 57th.

jokes.text: Ann says 'Piece of cake' then immediately panic-realizes 'Oh, we have to get the wedding cake. I'll do that too.'
jokes.setup: Ann confidently says 'piece of cake' as an idiom to mean the hair/makeup/dress job is manageable
jokes.punchline: She catches herself and takes it literally — there is no wedding cake, and she now has another task
jokes.explanation: A clean wordplay/literal misunderstanding joke. Not especially original — the 'idiom taken literally' structure is common — but it's executed quickly and adds to the comedic escalation of everything Ann has to do. Functional and charming.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I need to know you're 100% committed to this. No backing out, no matter what.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I was the one who suggested it in the first place.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Of course I'm committed.

jokes.text: Ann's talking head: 'I feel like every crazy thing Leslie's ever had me do has been like a drill, and today is the real thing. I'm ready, because I had the greatest teacher in the world. Leslie. Who is crazy.'
jokes.setup: Ann delivers an earnest, swelling speech about being prepared for this moment because of Leslie's training
jokes.punchline: The 'greatest teacher' reveal is Leslie — immediately undermined by '...who is crazy'
jokes.explanation: The talking-head structure is used perfectly here. The mock-heroic build-up ('greatest teacher in the world') followed by the flat tag ('who is crazy') is a classic Parks and Rec confessional rhythm. Ann's love and exasperation for Leslie are captured simultaneously. The economy of the tag is excellent — just two words, but they recontextualize the entire speech.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, we can't see each other before the wedding! That's bad luck!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, we live together.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, but it's bad luck!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You literally just saw me getting out of the shower.

jokes.text: Tom offers to get the marriage license, saying 'I got a guy that works at City Hall' — then Chris corrects 'That guy's my wife' — then Tom adds 'Um, you also work there.'
jokes.setup: Tom dramatically offers to source the marriage license via his 'guy' at City Hall, implying a shady connection
jokes.punchline: Chris reveals the 'guy' is actually his wife (Ann), and Tom awkwardly notes that Chris himself also works there — undermining the mystique entirely
jokes.explanation: A three-beat joke that works efficiently. Tom's posturing about 'having a guy' is classic Tom Haverford, Chris calling Ann his 'wife' (sweetly, characteristically) deflates it, and Tom's clueless 'also you work there' is a perfect anticlimactic button. All three characters are in voice.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I've been thinking... maybe you should change your last name to Wyatt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Ben, no. I'm Leslie Knope. I've built my entire career as Leslie Knope.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, I know. But think about it — you could be Leslie Wyatt. You could give up your job, your accomplishments, your identity as we know it, and just become Mrs. Ben Wyatt.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's insane.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Is it though?

jokes.text: Ron says walking Leslie down the aisle 'would be an honor, and the first time I won't regret walking down the aisle'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks Ron to walk her down the aisle. This is a tender, emotional ask.
jokes.punchline: Ron's acceptance is warm — then immediately darkened by the implication that both of his previous marriages were mistakes he regrets
jokes.explanation: This is among the best jokes in the episode. It works on three simultaneous levels: (1) genuine emotional warmth — Ron is honored; (2) a dark joke about his disastrous marriages; (3) perfectly in character — Ron never elaborates, never over-explains, just drops it and moves on. The economy is immaculate. The audience gets the full meaning from a single subordinate clause. This is exactly how Ron Swanson jokes should work, and it earns its 8+ rating.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, I need you to change your last name to Wyatt. I'm serious.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? Ben, no. I'm not changing my name.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'm just kidding. I was testing you.

jokes.text: The reaction beat: 'Oh, uh, yikes.' after Ron's marriage comment
jokes.setup: Ron's darkly funny comment about not regretting this aisle walk hangs in the air
jokes.punchline: Ben's single-word horrified reaction: 'Oh, uh, yikes.' — acknowledging the darkness without dwelling on it
jokes.explanation: A necessary comedic buffer after Ron's joke — the 'yikes' reaction validates the audience's reaction and keeps the scene moving. Not independently funny, but serves the structure. Ben is a reliable straight man here.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Go! Run! Get out of here!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Where am I running to?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: RUN!

jokes.text: Tom offers to be officiant with a 'Steve Harvey vibe or straight-up Seacrest?' pitch, then decides to combine them: 'Steve-crest'
jokes.setup: Tom volunteers to become an ordained minister online and immediately turns it into a branding exercise
jokes.punchline: The fusion name 'Steve-crest' — treating celebrity emcee styles like a product mashup
jokes.explanation: Very Tom Haverford — he can't resist aestheticizing and branding everything, even a sacred ceremony. The specific choices (Steve Harvey and Ryan Seacrest as his wedding emcee reference points) are funny because they're distinctly not the prestige choices. 'Steve-crest' as a portmanteau is quick and satisfying.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, from this moment forward, we go dark. We are now Operation Wedding Bells.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, it's just wedding planning.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Negative. You are now Agent Bridesmaid. I am Agent Groom Protector. We communicate only in code.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: This is ridiculous.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: The flowers have arrived. I repeat, the flowers have arrived. Initiating Phase Two.

jokes.text: Andy finds rings that turn out to be former nipple rings — revealed to have been the pawn shop owner's
jokes.setup: Andy finds rings he thinks are 'not bad' — 'real nice' — in the pawn shop tray
jokes.punchline: The owner reveals they were nipple rings. Andy asks 'How do you know?' The owner's silence (implied) leads April to flatly confirm: 'They were his.'
jokes.explanation: A clean escalating joke with a great three-beat structure: discovery → suspicion → confirmation. Andy's earnest 'How do you know?' is the key — he's genuinely curious, not horrified. April's deadpan 'They were his' is the perfect button. The comedy comes from the escalation from 'nice rings' to 'nipple rings' to 'his nipple rings' with no editorializing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I want to look like a cross between Margaret Thatcher, Ronald Reagan, and Golda Meir. Like, Thatcher's hair, Reagan's tan, and Meir's pantsuit.

jokes.text: Andy announces he's about to become a cop and declares he should 'commit as many crimes as possible tonight, get it out of my system'
jokes.setup: Andy mentions he's reporting for police duty tomorrow
jokes.punchline: His response to this responsibility is to pre-emptively commit crimes as a last hurrah — completely backwards logic delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy Dwyer logic — he arrives at completely wrong conclusions through sincere, earnest reasoning. The joke is that he's not being rebellious or ironic; he genuinely thinks this is the responsible thing to do before becoming a cop. The character integration is very high.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie prepared me for this moment. She said, 'Ann, you're going to be amazing. You're smart, you're beautiful, you're going to change the world.' It was so sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Then she grabbed my shoulders and said, 'But if you mess this up, I will actually lose my mind. Like, certifiably insane. They will have to medicate me.'

jokes.text: April steals ALL the marriage licenses so 'no one else in this town can get married, because it makes it less special for us'
jokes.setup: They've found the marriage licenses at City Hall
jokes.punchline: April announces she's taking all of them — not out of theft, but out of a possessive desire to make Leslie's marriage uniquely exclusive in Pawnee
jokes.explanation: Peak April Ludgate — casually committing a government crime with a logic that is simultaneously sweet (she loves Leslie) and deeply antisocial (she's stealing civil documents). Chris's 'Good call, babe' validates the absurdity. The reasoning is detailed enough to be funny: she doesn't want *other* marriages to dilute the specialness. It's weirdly touching and weird.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I have a guy at City Hall.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You work at City Hall.

jokes.text: And they were nipple rings, at one point. / How do you know that? / [beat] / They were his.
jokes.setup: Ben and April find what seem like decent rings; the clerk casually mentions they were nipple rings
jokes.punchline: Ben asks how the clerk knows — implying a dark answer — and the clerk confirms they were HIS nipple rings
jokes.explanation: The structure here is excellent: the pause between 'How do you know that?' and 'They were his' is the joke — the audience fills in the horrifying implication before the answer arrives. The misdirection and the cringe factor are both working. Impact is high because a room would erupt at 'They were his.'

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I would be honored. I've walked three women down the aisle before. They all left me, but I have no doubt that Ben will stay with you.

jokes.text: Leslie's outrage that the seamstress didn't finish the dress 'three months early' — 'if you're not gonna finish something three months early, then don't accept the job'
jokes.setup: The wedding dress isn't finished — a problem for an impromptu same-night wedding
jokes.punchline: Leslie's complaint isn't that it's not ready today; it's that it wasn't finished three months ahead of the May date — revealing her extreme type-A early-completion standards
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The entire comedy comes from the specificity: Leslie isn't complaining the dress isn't done for tonight's impromptu wedding — she's complaining it wasn't done THREE MONTHS before the planned May date. This is perfectly Leslie: her standard for preparedness is so extreme that the current failure (not done months early) is the real scandal. Could only be Leslie's line. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm gonna be like Steve Harvey and Ryan Seacrest combined. I'll call myself Stevacrest.

jokes.text: Leslie's suggestion: 'How did Cinderella finish her dress so fast?' Answer: 'Squirrels and birds.' — 'That's not very helpful.'
jokes.setup: Desperate for solutions to finish the wedding dress in time
jokes.punchline: Leslie sincerely floats a fairy-tale solution; Ann plays it straight ('squirrels and birds'); both immediately acknowledge it's not helpful
jokes.explanation: A quick absurdist exchange — the joke is that both women take it seriously enough to answer before dismissing it. The economy is excellent; the whole bit is four lines. Slightly below the episode's best because the premise (fairy-tale logic in real life) is a well-worn comedy beat.

dialogue.speaker: Store clerk
dialogue.line: The jewelry section is over there. Fair warning though - we just got a shipment of actual nails mixed in with the costume jewelry, so watch out for those.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'No time for verbs' while delegating tasks at speed
jokes.setup: Leslie is rapidly assigning tasks — 'Ann, dress duty. April and Andy, license duty.'
jokes.punchline: She self-narrates that she's speaking in a truncated grammar by announcing 'No time for verbs.'
jokes.explanation: A brilliant micro-joke. The humor is that Leslie is so self-aware of her own speech patterns that she meta-narrates them — but the meta-narration itself uses no verbs, making it both a description and an example of the phenomenon simultaneously. The economy is near-perfect: three words do a huge amount of work. Very quotable and deeply Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Store clerk
dialogue.line: These rings look really nice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Those are Andy's former nipple rings.

jokes.text: The Indiana celebrity look-alike gala: Orville Redenbacher, La Toya Jackson, Axl Rose, David Letterman
jokes.setup: The gala where Leslie and Ben are attending features Indiana-themed entertainment
jokes.punchline: The entertainment turns out to be celebrity look-alikes of Indiana celebrities — a hyperspecific and deliberately obscure list
jokes.explanation: The comedy is in the commitment to the bit — Indiana's celebrity roster is deliberately C-list nationally (Orville Redenbacher, La Toya Jackson instead of Michael), and the show treats them with the same reverence as A-listers. Pawnee-specific worldbuilding that rewards fans of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I'm becoming a cop tomorrow, so tonight I'm gonna commit as many crimes as possible.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's not how that works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Once I'm a cop, I can't break the law anymore. So I gotta get it all out of my system tonight.

jokes.text: The Li'l Sebastian look-alike announcement at the gala — Donna has booked 'a Li'l Sebastian look-alike on the way'
jokes.setup: Donna mentions the celebrity look-alike lineup at the gala
jokes.punchline: The punchline is the addition of a Li'l Sebastian look-alike — a miniature horse — to the list of human celebrity impersonators, treated with the same gravity
jokes.explanation: The joke lands hardest for longtime viewers — the idea that Li'l Sebastian is a 'celebrity' worthy of a look-alike is the show's most beloved running gag made meta. Donna's awed reaction to her own booking ('what? Oh my G--') and Jerry's speechless response set up the big emotional payoff when 'Bucky' the look-alike appears. The impact is elevated by the show's mythology.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm going to take all the marriage licenses.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not being selfish. I just want to prevent other people from getting married.

jokes.text: Jerry's reaction to the Li'l Sebastian news causes him to wet himself — 'Did you just pee your pants? Just a dab.' / 'You nasty, Jerry. Third time this week.'
jokes.setup: The Li'l Sebastian look-alike announcement overwhelms Jerry emotionally/physically
jokes.punchline: Jerry has urinated himself. His defense: 'Just a dab.' Donna's response: 'Third time this week.'
jokes.explanation: Jerry's humiliation is a running gag of the show, but this iteration has two great escalation beats: 'just a dab' (Jerry's dignity-preserving minimization) and 'Third time this week' (Donna casually revealing this is a pattern). The economy is excellent — Donna doesn't editorialize beyond 'you nasty,' which is exactly right.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need this dress finished by tomorrow morning.

dialogue.speaker: Seamstress
dialogue.line: Tomorrow morning? That's impossible. I need at least a week.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A week? I need it by 6 AM. I have a breakfast meeting at 6:15.

jokes.text: Tom's minister certification won't arrive for 24 hours — 'But this is America. I want it now!'
jokes.setup: Tom tries to get ordained online to officiate the wedding but the email confirmation takes 24 hours
jokes.punchline: His outrage is framed as a patriotic right: instant gratification is American
jokes.explanation: A solid character joke — Tom's consumer entitlement framed as American values is consistent with his character. The line 'But this is America' is a well-worn comedic trope, so the originality is limited, but the delivery context (ordination, not a product) gives it a small twist.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, I need a dress for the gala and I have nothing to wear.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: A fairy godmother could appear and transform rags into a beautiful gown.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ann, that's not helpful. I need an actual solution.

jokes.text: Tom reveals his wedding officiant speech has 'six guaranteed applause breaks' and includes a beatbox and dance breakdown
jokes.setup: Tom is disappointed he can't officiate, because he'd prepared material
jokes.punchline: The material turns out to be a full performance piece with 'six guaranteed applause breaks' — treating a wedding ceremony like a variety show
jokes.explanation: Very Tom Haverford — he's incapable of doing anything without turning it into a showcase. The specific detail of 'six guaranteed applause breaks' is funny because of the precision (not 'a few,' not 'several,' specifically six, and they're guaranteed). Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I can forge the signature. I do it all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What? Really?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's not that hard. I've forged my parents' signatures since I was twelve.

jokes.text: Jerry reveals he's actually ordained — 'That's the worst idea I've ever heard.' / 'Yeah, you're right, okay.' / 'Wait! What if you do the ceremony but don't have any stupid ideas of your own...'
jokes.setup: Jerry offers his ordination as a solution
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately shoots it down as the worst idea ever — then a beat later comes back with a 'compromise' that is just Jerry doing Tom's vision with none of Jerry's input
jokes.explanation: Good Tom/Jerry dynamic. Tom's self-serving 'compromise' ('you do the ceremony but say only my stuff') is a perfect encapsulation of his narcissism. Jerry's willingness to go along with it 'anything to help Leslie' is poignant and funny simultaneously. The reversal — shooting it down then immediately pivoting — is a strong structural choice.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you take the permits. Ann, venue coordination. Tom, catering. Jerry, you're on... wait, what can Jerry do? Just stand there. Stand there, Jerry. Jerry stand.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And stop talking in complete sentences everyone. No time. We abbreviate. 'The thing' instead of 'the thing that we discussed.' 'Donna did the stuff' instead of 'Donna completed the tasks assigned to her.' Pronouns optional. Articles eliminated. Verbs becoming suggestions.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm not even sure words need to be real anymore. 'Ron spreadsheet the budget-ify.' Everyone understand? No? Good. Less time explaining, more time doing.

jokes.text: Tom's speech opens with Will Smith's monologue from 'the modern cinematic classic... Hitch'
jokes.setup: Tom is revealing the content of his wedding speech to Jerry
jokes.punchline: The opening of his lovingly crafted ceremony is a verbatim Will Smith monologue from the romantic comedy Hitch — called 'a modern cinematic classic' with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: The comedic payload is entirely in Tom's sincere reverence for Hitch as 'a modern cinematic classic' — an objective characterization of a mid-tier Will Smith rom-com. This is peak Tom Haverford taste-making. The joke doesn't require you to know Hitch; it works purely on Tom's unironic elevation of it. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You just said 'touch base' and 'boil the ocean' in the same sentence. I'm not sure what you're trying to do, but I want no part of it.

jokes.text: Ben's rings update: 'No rings, just a tennis bracelet and a necklace that says Wine Chick'
jokes.setup: Ben reports back on the ring search from Ann's house
jokes.punchline: The specificity of what he did find: a 'Wine Chick' necklace — the exact kind of kitschy item you'd find in a box of Ann Perkins's old stuff
jokes.explanation: The specificity sells it — 'Wine Chick' is the exact right level of cringe-cute for Ann Perkins's jewelry box. Ben deadpanning the inventory is good straight-man work. Sets up Leslie's critique of Ann's taste.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: We got Li'l Sebastian!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: *looks shocked, then visibly pees himself*

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Ann Perkins has terrible taste in rings. What is this? A toe ring with a brown gemstone? Is this a ruby that's gone bad?'
jokes.setup: Leslie examines the rings Ben found in Ann's old box of things
jokes.punchline: Her specific horror at a 'toe ring with a brown gemstone' and the concept of a 'ruby that's gone bad' — applying food-spoilage logic to a gemstone
jokes.explanation: The gem of this joke is 'a ruby that's gone bad' — treating a gemstone with the concerned logic of checking produce for spoilage. It's a small, perfectly worded absurdist observation. Leslie's exasperated love for Ann (insulting her taste while desperately needing her help) is a great character note throughout the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Did you just pee yourself?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: A little bit.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Jerry, you pee yourself like once a week.

jokes.text: No rings, no license, no dress. This idea felt so right, but maybe it's just too crazy. Maybe it wasn't meant to be.
jokes.setup: All the wedding logistics have fallen apart simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Ben's quiet resignation — 'maybe it wasn't meant to be' — is understated comedy because the audience is ahead of him: of course it IS meant to be (it's a sitcom wedding episode)
jokes.explanation: Functional dramatic beat with mild comedy in the understatement. Not a strong joke on its own — more of a structural pivot point. Below average for this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've been on this website for twenty minutes and I still don't have my ordination certificate. What is this, communist Russia?

jokes.text: Bucky the Li'l Sebastian impersonator is introduced — 'He's a licensed Li'l Sebastian impersonator'
jokes.setup: Something white appears in the snow, mystically, while Leslie is despairing — she believes it's a sign
jokes.punchline: It's not Li'l Sebastian returned from the dead — it's Bucky, a 'licensed Li'l Sebastian impersonator,' arriving for the gala
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's biggest comedy moments. The structure is perfect: emotional despair → mysterious white shape in the snow → genuine hope/belief → comedic deflation with a mundane explanation ('licensed Li'l Sebastian impersonator'). The word 'licensed' is doing enormous work — it implies a regulatory body, a test, an industry. For Parks and Rec fans, the idea that Li'l Sebastian has reached the level of requiring licensed impersonators is simultaneously absurd and deeply of this show's world. High impact for the fan audience.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I was really looking forward to officiating your wedding. I had this whole thing planned out. I was gonna do a bit where I come down the aisle on a zip line.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Then I'm gonna do a backflip off the altar. Then I'm gonna pull out a flaming saxophone and just shred for like twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: And then at the end, I'm gonna say 'By the power vested in me by the state of Indiana and also by Nicki Minaj, I now pronounce you husband and wife.'

jokes.text: Leslie declares 'This is Li'l Sebastian, and this is a sign' — to an actual horse impersonator named Bucky
jokes.setup: The handler has just clarified this is Bucky, a look-alike, not Li'l Sebastian
jokes.punchline: Leslie ignores the correction entirely and wills it to be Li'l Sebastian because she needs the sign
jokes.explanation: The joke is Leslie's complete refusal to accept the factual correction. The handler protests 'Actually, this is Bucky' and Leslie simply overrides it: 'Quiet, you. This is Li'l Sebastian.' Her closing 'Yes, ma'am' from the handler is perfect — he gives up. This captures Leslie's brand of loving irrationality that makes her character so beloved.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to have Hitch playing at my wedding ceremony. It's high art.

jokes.text: Come on, Bucky. / Li'l Sebastian. / Yes, ma'am.
jokes.setup: Leslie has declared Bucky to be Li'l Sebastian and is rallying the group
jokes.punchline: When she corrects the wrangler's use of 'Bucky,' he immediately and meekly capitulates with 'Yes, ma'am' — Leslie's force of personality conquering even a stranger
jokes.explanation: The button on the Li'l Sebastian bit. The wrangler's immediate submission to Leslie's reality is a great grace note — 'yes, ma'am' is exactly right. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Okay, so we have code words for the wedding. If I say 'waffles,' that means we need to talk about the venue.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Waffles! I love waffles!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, Andy, it's a code word.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Right, right. So if you say 'waffles,' you want waffles.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, waffles means venue.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A waffle venue? That's actually genius!

jokes.text: Leslie asks Ann to have 'sewn a new dress from scratch' or 'several dresses, cause I would love some options'
jokes.setup: Leslie desperately calls Ann for a dress update
jokes.punchline: She's not asking if Ann has a solution — she's asking if Ann has made multiple dresses so Leslie can choose among options, within a one-hour window
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'made a dress' to 'made several dresses for options' in a single sentence is very Leslie. She can't help herself — even in crisis, her standards are impossibly high. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Ann's Project Runway pitch — 'I've been watching a lot of Project Runway recently... In the past eight years.' Then Leslie: 'No time to do the Tim Gunn voice... Wait, what am I talking about? There's always time. Designers, make it work.'
jokes.setup: Ann says she's been watching Project Runway as a credential for designing a dress
jokes.punchline: Leslie starts to say there's no time for a Tim Gunn impression — then immediately contradicts herself and does it anyway, because some things are non-negotiable
jokes.explanation: The joke has a beautiful internal structure: setup (Ann's 'credentials'), false start (no time for Tim Gunn), immediate reversal ('what am I talking about'), and payoff (she does the bit anyway). Leslie's recognition that some things transcend urgency — doing the Tim Gunn voice is one of them — is perfectly in character. The self-correction is the funniest part.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is that...? Li'l Sebastian!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Wait, that can't be. Li'l Sebastian passed away.

dialogue.speaker: Horse handler
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm a certified Li'l Sebastian impersonator. I have my professional licensing and everything.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Professional licensing? For impersonating a horse?

dialogue.speaker: Horse handler
dialogue.line: It's a very specific skill set.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I... I can't believe this.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'No time to do the Tim Gunn voice. Wait, what am I talking about? There's always time. Designers, make it work.'
jokes.setup: Leslie references Tim Gunn's famous catchphrase in the context of Project Runway
jokes.punchline: She catches herself, reverses course, and delivers the voice anyway — because even in crisis, Leslie cannot resist a bit
jokes.explanation: A lovely self-aware Leslie moment. The joke is in the reversal — she can't help herself, even knowing it's inappropriate timing. The self-contradiction ('no time' → 'there's ALWAYS time') is well-structured and very Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, is that... is that Li'l Sebastian?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is a sign. This is the universe telling me that everything is going to be okay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Li'l Sebastian has spoken.

jokes.text: April and Chris wake up City Clerk Ethel Beavers at 10pm — she says she's been asleep for four hours and was on a date, he's sleeping over
jokes.setup: They desperately need Ethel's signature on the marriage license and show up at her house at 10pm
jokes.punchline: She's been asleep since 6pm — and her 'sleeping over' guest isn't a husband, it was a successful first date
jokes.explanation: A pleasant character surprise — elderly Ethel Beavers, previously established as a crotchety bureaucrat, turns out to have an active dating life. April's 'Cool.' response to the sleeping-over news is a perfect deadpan. Not a huge laugh but a solid warm character moment with a genuine surprise.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm going to channel my inner Tim Gunn. Make it work!

jokes.text: April and Chris ask Ethel to be their 'adopted grandma' — 'Can we adopt you as our grandma? Fine. Cool! We love you, Grandma!'
jokes.setup: Ethel signs the license; April and Chris gush about her house, nightgown, and dating ability
jokes.punchline: The compliments spontaneously escalate into an impromptu grandma adoption that Ethel accepts with one word
jokes.explanation: The joke is the casualness of the adoption — they ask ('Can we adopt you?'), she says 'Fine,' they immediately celebrate ('We love you, Grandma!'). The speed at which this grandmother relationship is formed and accepted by all parties is the comedy. Also funny that this comes from Chris and April, an unlikely duo. Ethel's complete unflappability ('Fine.') is the best beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We need to wake up the city clerk. It's an emergency.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We've been knocking for ten minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What? What time is it?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's 9 PM.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: 9 PM?! That's the middle of the night!

jokes.text: Tom's speech line: 'When I heard Ben was getting married, I was like, to Leslie or to Game of Thrones?'
jokes.setup: Tom reveals his wedding speech material to Jerry
jokes.punchline: The opening joke implies Ben's relationship with Game of Thrones is as serious as his relationship with Leslie — a nerd joke delivered as a roast opener
jokes.explanation: A solid character joke about Ben's nerdiness — the Game of Thrones reference is accurate to Ben's character, and the roast-joke structure is appropriate for a wedding speech. Not exceptional but well-targeted at Ben specifically.

jokes.text: 'You mad sweet on that back meat' — Tom's speech line about Leslie talking about Ben's butt
jokes.setup: Tom's speech includes a bit about Leslie's obsession with Ben's posterior, written in Tom's signature vernacular
jokes.punchline: 'Back meat' as a term for buttocks — delivered as though it's an elegant turn of phrase worth putting in a wedding ceremony
jokes.explanation: The term 'back meat' is the joke — Tom's linguistic creativity in coining a phrase that is somehow both cruder and more clinical than 'butt' is peak Tom Haverford. The fact that he considers this wedding-speech-worthy, and calls it 'beautiful words,' adds the second layer. 'Back meat' specifically achieves high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You know what? You have really nice hands. Like, really nice hands for holding someone's face while you kiss them.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: And I bet you're great at knowing exactly when to text someone back. Not too eager, not too aloof.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your shoulders probably look really good in a t-shirt. The kind of t-shirt that says 'I'm casual but also I care about my appearance.'

jokes.text: Jerry's announcement to the gala that there'll be a wedding at 11:01 with 'all the drinks and the food will be on us'
jokes.setup: Jerry gets on a microphone to announce the surprise wedding to gala guests
jokes.punchline: He offers free drinks and food — generosity that presumably belongs to Leslie and the city, not Jerry personally, and that they likely haven't authorized
jokes.explanation: A mild laugh — Jerry going slightly off-script by giving away free things is in character, but the joke isn't sharp enough to be memorable. Works as a scene beat more than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Is this... is this cubic zirconia?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's a family heirloom.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Right, but it's fake, though.

jokes.text: Councilman Jamm's megaphone heckling outside the gala: 'Boo, Leslie Knope, boo.' then his dental practice ad-lib: 'Hey, butter-teeth, what's up? I can fix those chompers for you. Just come to Jamm Orthodontics.'
jokes.setup: Jamm is outside the gala protesting the park with a megaphone
jokes.punchline: Mid-protest, he pivots to advertising his orthodontics practice at a random bystander — confusing political activism with guerrilla marketing
jokes.explanation: The comedy is Jamm's inability to separate his political vendetta from his business interests — even while loudly protesting, he spots a marketing opportunity and pivots seamlessly to 'butter-teeth.' The specific insult ('butter-teeth') and the casual product placement mid-tantrum are excellent character details. Jamm is a perfectly conceived petty villain.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: We could melt down Ann's light fixture.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Jamm she's getting married in a half-hour 'to the most perfect man in the world' and ends with 'Knope rules, Jamm sucks'
jokes.setup: Leslie confronts Jamm outside the gala during the chaos
jokes.punchline: She closes her impassioned speech about her perfect night with the playground-level taunt 'Knope rules, Jamm sucks'
jokes.explanation: The joke is the tonal drop from romantic proclamation to schoolyard chant. Leslie builds to the emotional peak ('most perfect man in the world,' 'all my dreams are coming true') and then immediately lands on 'Knope rules, Jamm sucks' — which sounds like she's been waiting all night to say it. Highly quotable, very Leslie.

jokes.text: Leslie, about to repeat the Jamm taunt in front of another councilman, course-corrects: 'Knope rules, Ja-- Councilman Howser.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is mid-chant as another authority figure appears
jokes.punchline: She catches herself halfway through the taunt and pivots to a formal greeting
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback that requires only three words to be funny ('Knope rules, Ja--'). The audience understands exactly what was about to be said, and the clean pivot to 'Councilman Howser' is the payoff. Economy is outstanding — the joke is in what isn't said. Rewatch value because you catch it differently each time.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Listen up! These so-called 'parks' are just wastelands for the lazy!

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: And another thing - they call it a 'park' but it's really a 'paaark'!

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: The government wants you thinking 'paaark' so you don't realize it's just dirt!

jokes.text: Ron breaks his 'not going to cry' promise five times, is consoled by Ben's dad-figure
jokes.setup: Ron has promised not to cry at the wedding
jokes.punchline: He confesses he's already broken that promise five times; Chris/Ben's father figure then immediately starts crying too
jokes.explanation: Ron crying is inherently funny because of his emotional armor. The escalation of 'five times' and the immediate transfer of crying to the next person is a solid running gag beat. Warm but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You know what? This wedding is a joke, just like your department. But speaking of jokes, have you considered switching to Jamm & Associates for your legal needs? We offer competitive rates and a proven track record of success.

jokes.text: Ben tells Ron he's 'transferring his crying thing' to him — Ron breaking down and saying 'it's okay buddy, let it out'
jokes.setup: Ron has made Ben emotional with his gift; Ben is fighting tears
jokes.punchline: The role reversal — Ron, the emotionally granite man, accuses Ben of 'transferring' his crying to Ron, then Ron himself is the one saying 'let it out, buddy' while presumably also crying
jokes.explanation: Seeing Ron Swanson cry — or being forced to admit he might cry — is high-value comedy because of how against type it is. 'Transferring your crying thing' is a beautifully Ron way to describe emotional contagion (he treats it like a virus). The reversal where he then says 'let it out, buddy' implies he himself is the one needing to let it out is excellent. Very high character integration — this scene only works with Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: How does it look?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's... it's very you. I mean, it's not very flattering, but it's very you.

jokes.text: Chris to Ben: 'Damn it, you're transferring your crying thing over to me.'
jokes.setup: Ben's emotion has been building through Chris's gift of the statehouse letter
jokes.punchline: Chris, who is typically the emotionally effusive one, blames Ben for 'transferring' tears — as if emotions are contagious and contractually his department
jokes.explanation: Chris's framing of crying as a transferable object is good character comedy — it's very Chris Traeger to apply an almost clinical framing to emotions. The role reversal (Chris telling Ben to control his emotions) is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Ben, when I first came to Pawnee, I thought it was the worst place on Earth. But then I met you, and Leslie, and everyone in this department. And I realized that Pawnee isn't a place—it's the people. You're my best friend, and I'm so grateful for this unexpected journey we've been on together.

jokes.text: Ann reveals the finished dress: 'It is like the Ann Perkins of dresses'
jokes.setup: Ann has made Leslie a dress from scratch and Leslie sees it
jokes.punchline: Leslie's ultimate compliment is to compare the dress to Ann herself — creating a recursive compliment that is either profound or nonsensical
jokes.explanation: This is one of the most beloved joke structures in Parks and Rec — Leslie complimenting Ann by comparing something to Ann herself. 'It is like the Ann Perkins of dresses' works because (a) it's a callback to Leslie's established habit of Ann-compliments, (b) it's logically circular but emotionally perfect, (c) it's extremely quotable, and (d) it captures the Leslie/Ann relationship in four words. The joke earns its high scores because it's deeply character-integrated, highly original as a comedic construction, and becomes a fan-favorite type of line. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, this dress is absolutely Ann.

jokes.text: Jamm's heckling version of the wedding march: '♪ Here comes the boo / All dressed in boo / Boo, Leslie Knope / Boo, boo-oo-oo-oo ♪'
jokes.setup: Leslie is walking to her wedding as Jamm heckles with a megaphone
jokes.punchline: Jamm has composed and is performing a full parody version of the wedding march in real time, replacing all words with 'boo'
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's best jokes. The commitment to the bit — Jamm doesn't just yell 'boo,' he constructs a proper parody of the Wedding March with correct syllable counts and a held note on 'boo-oo-oo-oo' — shows a level of petty craft that elevates him from villain to comedic genius. It's also funnier because he must have prepared this, meaning he anticipated this opportunity. The joke works on the absurdist level (who does this) and the character level (Jamm would absolutely do this). Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, I can't see Ann before the meeting. That's bad luck!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not a real thing.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, you don't know that. What if I see Tom? That's double bad luck. What if I see Jerry? That's triple bad luck. What if I see all three of you at once? I think the building explodes.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: The building doesn't explode.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You don't know that!

jokes.text: Jamm deploys a stink bomb at Leslie's wedding, purchased on Amazon Prime with free two-day shipping
jokes.setup: Jamm escalates from heckling to a physical attack at the wedding
jokes.punchline: The weapon of choice is a stink bomb — and his proud boast is that he's an Amazon Prime customer who got free two-day shipping
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: (1) a stink bomb is a child's weapon being used in adult political sabotage; (2) Jamm is proud of his Prime membership specifically in this context; (3) 'You are looking at a prime customer, everybody' is delivered to a crowd at a wedding as a genuine flex. The mundane pride in Amazon Prime membership during a villainous act is the key comedic element. Very Jamm.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: Boo! Boo! Boooo!

jokes.text: Ron punching Jamm in the teeth at the wedding — breaking his tooth — then Jamm saying 'Well, good thing you're an orthodontist'
jokes.setup: Ron handles the Jamm situation physically — punching him in the mouth
jokes.punchline: Jamm's tooth breaks. Jamm points out: 'Well, good thing you're an orthodontist' — his own profession making this injury professionally convenient
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best physical comedy moment and possibly its best single joke. The structure is perfect: Ron punches Jamm (audience satisfaction), tooth breaks, and then Jamm's recovery line — 'Well, good thing you're an orthodontist' — is brilliant because it's completely true, it's Jamm finding a silver lining in his own dental trauma, and it recontextualizes Ron's punch as inadvertently helpful to Jamm's practice. The joke also lands on Leslie's delighted 'Yay, best wedding ever.' Ron's deadpan 'Yeah, it is a good thing' completing the exchange is excellent. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You know what? I have Amazon Prime. Two-day shipping, baby!

jokes.text: Leslie insisting Ron must be present to walk her down the aisle: 'I lost my father when I was ten, I don't have any brothers, and Ken Burns never wrote me back.'
jokes.setup: Ron has punched Jamm and is in police custody; Leslie refuses to get married without him
jokes.punchline: Her list of reasons she needs Ron — absent father, no brothers — escalates to the absurdist specific: Ken Burns never wrote her back, placing the documentary filmmaker in the same category as family
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode and among the best Leslie Knope lines of the series. The structure is a classic triple with a devastating subversion: 'I lost my father' (genuine emotion), 'I don't have any brothers' (more genuine emotion), 'and Ken Burns never wrote me back' (complete tonal collapse into absurdist comedy). The Ken Burns reference is perfect Leslie: she wrote to a documentary filmmaker as a potential father figure/brother surrogate, and his not responding is placed in the same emotional register as losing a parent. The economy is immaculate — no explanation needed, no punchline tagged on. The specificity of 'Ken Burns' (not 'a filmmaker' or 'a director') is essential. This earns its highest score.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Well, you're a dentist. Isn't that a little ironic?

jokes.text: Jamm: 'You broke my tooth.' / Ron: 'Well, good thing you're an orthodontist.' / Jamm: 'Yeah, it is a good thing. You see my house? Five bathrooms.'
jokes.setup: Jamm complains Ron broke his tooth from the punch
jokes.punchline: Ron's comeback is perfect; Jamm's response is to brag about his house and its five bathrooms — completely unfazed by the injury or the circumstances
jokes.explanation: The episode's peak joke. Three-beat perfection: (1) Jamm's complaint, (2) Ron's immediately devastating and logical comeback ('good thing you're an orthodontist'), (3) Jamm's bizarre non-sequitur pivot to bragging about his five-bathroom house as proof he's fine. Each beat is better than the last. Jamm's non-sequitur house brag is inspired — it reveals he processes everything through status signaling. Ron's line is perfectly economical. This is legitimately exceptional sitcom writing. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor or above.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, you have to be at my wedding. First, you're my best friend. Second, I need someone to give me away who won't cry, and third... Ken Burns rejected you as a documentary filmmaker.

jokes.text: Yeah, it is a good thing. / You see my house? Five bathrooms.
jokes.setup: Ron has pointed out that Jamm can fix his own tooth since he's an orthodontist
jokes.punchline: Jamm agrees — then immediately pivots to bragging about his five-bathroom house, apparently trying to assert dominance while bleeding from a punch
jokes.explanation: Jamm bragging about five bathrooms while nursing a punch-induced dental injury is a masterpiece of comic pathos. He's trying to win a status battle immediately after losing a physical one, using the only metric he has. 'Five bathrooms' becomes an absurdly funny status symbol. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: He's a psychopath mastermind. He's like an armless murderer.

dialogue.speaker: Chief Jim Dunn
dialogue.line: How would he murder anyone if he has no arms?

jokes.text: Ron's apology: 'I've never presented a bride on her wedding day... I don't think you're supposed to punch a man in the mouth during the service.' / Leslie: 'I think that's exactly what you're supposed to do, if that mouth is attached to a drunk jerk-face.'
jokes.setup: Ron apologizes for punching Jamm during Leslie's wedding
jokes.punchline: Leslie's response completely vindicates Ron — and her coinage of 'drunk jerk-face' as a formal category of person makes it funnier
jokes.explanation: The exchange is warm and funny. Ron's formal framing of 'presenting a bride' for the duties of walking someone down the aisle is good, and Leslie's enthusiastic vindication using 'drunk jerk-face' as a defined legal category is the button.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been in this cell for three hours, and I've already figured out the bathroom situation. There are TWO toilets on this block. TWO. Do you know how many bathrooms I have at home? Seventeen. SEVENTEEN. That's how you measure success in this world.

jokes.text: Andy at the police station imagining his detective career: the criminal 'chopped off both his arms so he wouldn't leave fingerprints' — 'Well, how did he murder the person?' — 'I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Andy is playing out a police procedural fantasy with Chris at the station, interrogating a 'psychopath'
jokes.punchline: The criminal's method of avoiding fingerprints — removing his own arms — raises an immediate logical problem: how did an armless man commit the murder? The Captain has no answer.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant logic-trap absurdism. The criminal has removed his own arms to avoid leaving fingerprints — a clever solution to one problem that creates an unsolvable second problem. The Captain confidently calls him 'a psychopath' who 'chopped off both arms' and then is completely stumped by the obvious follow-up question ('Well, how did he murder the person?'). The 'I don't know' is the perfect answer — honest, flat, and devastating. This is the kind of absurdist comedy that reveals genuine comedic intelligence. Earns 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what I love about government buildings? The fluorescent lighting. It's so romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's not romantic at all.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And the beige walls? The filing cabinets? The faint smell of old paper and broken dreams? It's beautiful.

jokes.text: Better get used to this, honey. Gonna be a lot of late nights for me here. Graveyard shift.
jokes.setup: Andy is pre-reporting to the police station before his first day
jokes.punchline: He's playacting at being a hardboiled cop — telling April to 'get used to' his long hours before he's even started — with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Andy's cop-show fantasizing is well-established character comedy. He's doing the movie version of being a cop before he's done any of the actual cop work. Solid but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: The ceremony is a disaster! I've got seventeen groomsmen, a string quartet playing remixes, and the aisle is lined with rose petals I had specially imported from—

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, just speak from the heart. That's all that matters.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, that's... actually good advice.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know. Surprising, right?

jokes.text: Andy's first question to the police chief: 'Is it a dog?' (about his new partner)
jokes.setup: The police chief mentions something about Andy's new partner
jokes.punchline: Andy's immediate first guess — and apparent greatest hope — is that his partner is a dog
jokes.explanation: Economy perfection — three words deliver a complete Andy Dwyer character portrait. His enthusiasm for having a dog partner, delivered as a sincere question, is immediately funny. The pause before it (implied by structure) makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Jamm in the jail cell insisting he's the victim: 'He punched me in the teeth. This is an outrage.' — Police response: 'Sleep it off in the cell, Councilman.'
jokes.setup: Jamm threw a stink bomb at a wedding and is now in a jail cell
jokes.punchline: He frames Ron's retaliatory punch as the real crime; the police dismiss him with perfect bureaucratic calm
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat — Jamm's aggrieved victimhood after his own escalating villainy is consistent, and 'sleep it off in the cell, Councilman' is a great dismissal. But the joke doesn't add much new to what we already know about Jamm. Functional scene closer.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I've traveled to 47 different countries for work. I thought I was just doing my job, being a public servant, going where I was needed. But now I realize... I was unconsciously searching for Leslie the whole time.

jokes.text: Ron's apology beat: 'I don't think you're supposed to punch a man in the mouth during the service.' Leslie: 'I think that's exactly what you're supposed to do, if that mouth is attached to a drunk jerk-face.'
jokes.setup: Ron apologizes to Leslie for the violence, framing it as a potential breach of wedding etiquette
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reframe: yes, punching IS appropriate wedding conduct — under specific conditions involving a 'drunk jerk-face'
jokes.explanation: Ron's formal, etiquette-based framing of punching someone ('I don't think you're supposed to') is very Ron — he's not apologizing for violence, he's concerned about protocol. Leslie's enthusiastic endorsement of the punch with the caveat 'jerk-face' is the right response. The word 'jerk-face' as Leslie's epithet is endearingly mild for the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I've written my vows. They're about 247 pages long.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: 247 pages?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I have a lot of feelings about you, Ben. And I needed to express all of them. Alphabetically, chronologically, and by theme.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, the ceremony is only three hours long.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know. I've also written a 92-page appendix in case I miss anything.

jokes.text: Ben: 'I got five bathrooms.' / Leslie: 'I love the first floor of City Hall at night. / Ron: 'I've never willingly been here later than 5:04 p.m.'
jokes.setup: The group is wrapping up and chatting as the gala is being dismantled
jokes.punchline: Jamm's five-bathroom house brag has propagated into the dialogue as a non-sequitur; Ron's 5:04 p.m. cutoff is hyper-specific and very Ron
jokes.explanation: The five-bathrooms callback is a light touch. Ron's 5:04 p.m. is a good character beat — the extra four minutes is a very Ron specificity. Leslie's love for City Hall at night is in-character but not particularly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, you are my soulmate, my best friend, and the love of my life. And I like you.

jokes.text: Ron's rare tender speech to Leslie before the ceremony — 'You are a wonderful person... you look very beautiful.' — Leslie: 'Okay, weirdo. Let's go.'
jokes.setup: Ron stops Leslie for a genuine emotional moment outside City Hall
jokes.punchline: After Ron delivers a beautiful, un-Ron speech, Leslie's response is 'Okay, weirdo. Let's go.' — treating his vulnerability with affectionate dismissal
jokes.explanation: The joke is that both characters are operating out of type: Ron is being openly sentimental, Leslie is being dismissive and calling him 'weirdo.' Yet it works because their relationship is established enough that 'weirdo' is entirely loving. The role reversal — Leslie usually being the gusher, Ron the stoic — gives the laugh. 'Okay, weirdo. Let's go.' is very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know what they say... when life gives you lemons, you make lemonade. When life gives you melons, you make... melonade? Is that a thing?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, wait, I got it. When one door closes, another door opens. Unless you're trapped in a room with no doors, then you have to gnaw through the drywall with your teeth until your gums bleed and you pass out from blood loss.

jokes.text: Tom's crisis: his speech is wrong — '20 minutes of Hitch quotes before I even say Leslie's name.' Jerry's advice: 'Speak from the heart.' Tom: 'Well, I'm not crazy about the part where you do something.'
jokes.setup: Tom realizes his speech is terrible and asks Jerry for help
jokes.punchline: Jerry suggests splitting duties — Tom does the speech, Jerry does the official parts — and Tom's 'compromise' negotiation is: 'Well, I'm not crazy about the part where you do something.'
jokes.explanation: Tom's negotiating position — grudging acceptance of Jerry participating while clearly not wanting him to have any role — is great character work. 'I'm not crazy about the part where you do something' is an extremely quotable formulation of dismissiveness. The self-awareness that his speech (20 minutes of Hitch quotes) is wrong is also funny.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Andy, you need to understand something. Life is about making choices. Real choices. Every single day you wake up, you're deciding who you want to be.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: He's been doing this for twenty minutes.

jokes.text: Jerry's officiating tone: 'It's been a long and winding road for these two lovebirds' — immediately followed by 'Yes, just do it already.'
jokes.setup: Jerry is officiating the ceremony, beginning with a standard platitude
jokes.punchline: A guest (possibly Tom) immediately calls out for the ceremony to just proceed, skipping the filler
jokes.explanation: A mild audience-surrogate joke — the impatient guest voices what viewers feel about overly long ceremony preambles. Functional but not particularly original.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We'll remember Li'l Sebastian, always in our hearts. You brought us joy and laughter. And now you're gone... you're gone forever. We'll miss you, little buddy. Rest in peace.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I see you in a meadow, running free. But then... then your legs fall off and turn into wings. Beautiful, majestic wings. And you fly away, but something's not right. Something's deeply, deeply wrong.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'I assume, and hope, you prepared your own vows?' and 'Ben, you want to say some stuff about Leslie?'
jokes.setup: Jerry is officiating a wedding he prepared for in minutes
jokes.punchline: His language is comically informal and nervous — 'I assume and hope' signals he doesn't know, 'say some stuff about Leslie' reduces wedding vows to a casual chat
jokes.explanation: Jerry's nervousness made manifest through deflated language is in character — he's winging it and knows it. 'Say some stuff about Leslie' is a charming understatement for a wedding vow. Works well as character-based situational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I just took apart the light fixture in my office, melted down the brass, and cast it into rings. It's not that hard. Any idiot can do it.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'Ben, you want to say some stuff about Leslie?'
jokes.setup: Jerry is officiating and needs to cue the vows
jokes.punchline: 'You want to say some stuff about Leslie?' — the most casual, inarticulate possible way to introduce wedding vows
jokes.explanation: Jerry reducing the solemnity of wedding vows to 'say some stuff about Leslie' is perfectly Jerry — he means well but the phrasing is magnificently deflating. Great economy.

jokes.text: Leslie reveals her vows were 70 pages long — written 'the day after we got engaged' — but she doesn't have them; suggests checking her office
jokes.setup: Leslie is asked to say her vows after Ben's beautiful impromptu speech
jokes.punchline: She has written 70-page vows — prepared the day after engagement — but doesn't have them now; somehow suggests there might be a copy in her nearby office
jokes.explanation: A 70-page vow written immediately after engagement is peak Leslie Knope overpreparedness. The added detail that she might have a copy filed at her office — the office that is in the building where she's currently getting married — is funny because she's not even ruling out pausing the ceremony to retrieve them. Ben's 'No. That's fine, that's fine.' is the perfect response. Very high character integration.

jokes.text: 'I love you and I like you.' — Leslie's vow punchline
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering improvised vows after acknowledging her 70-page prepared version isn't available
jokes.punchline: After a series of genuine, moving statements about Ben's support, she lands on 'I love you and I like you.' — the addition of 'and I like you' doing unexpected heavy lifting
jokes.explanation: This is the best line in the episode and one of the best lines in Parks and Recreation's run. 'I love you and I like you' works as comedy and as genuine sentiment simultaneously. The joke: everyone says 'I love you' at weddings — adding 'and I like you' implies that love alone isn't sufficient and that actual liking is a separate, meaningful upgrade. The comedy is that it sounds like a lesser compliment (you also... like him?) but is actually the greater one — it reflects Leslie's belief that being someone's best friend is the highest form of love. It's simultaneously funny, quotable, and deeply character-true. Perfect economy — six words. This is a 9+ joke.

jokes.text: Jerry: 'You may now kiss the--' then the couple immediately kisses before he finishes, cutting him off: 'Well, oops, okay.'
jokes.setup: Jerry is about to deliver the traditional 'you may now kiss the bride' line
jokes.punchline: Ben and Leslie jump the gun; Jerry's response — 'Well, oops, okay.' — is both a non-response and perfectly in character
jokes.explanation: A well-executed situational gag. Jerry being cut off is a mild indignity but also shows how eager Ben and Leslie are. 'Well, oops, okay.' is perfectly Jerry — accepting his marginalization with good nature. The economy of the reaction is good. Classic wedding sitcom beat but played with genuine warmth.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Lagavulin all around? Don't bother answering. I am already pouring.' / Then to April: 'You don't have to drink yours.' / 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: Celebration immediately after the ceremony
jokes.punchline: Ron has his Scotch pre-poured before anyone responds — and his one concession to April's age/taste is a quiet 'you don't have to drink yours' / 'thank you.' beat
jokes.explanation: Very Ron — he doesn't ask what people want, he just pours what he considers correct (Lagavulin). 'Don't bother answering' is the right level of benevolent dictatorship. The quiet Ron/April beat ('you don't have to drink yours' / 'Thank you') is a small, perfect character moment — Ron's minimal accommodation of others, April's terse gratitude.

jokes.text: Ron: 'Lagavulin all around? Don't bother answering. I am already pouring.' / Chris: 'You don't have to drink yours.' / Ron: 'Thank you.'
jokes.setup: The wedding is over and Ron immediately produces Scotch
jokes.punchline: Ron doesn't even wait for agreement — he's pouring regardless. Chris's accommodation of Ron's non-drinking (presumably offering the Scotch to someone else) and Ron's simple 'Thank you' is a good beat.
jokes.explanation: Very Ron. The preemptive pouring ('don't bother answering') is his character in one action. The exchange with Chris about not having to drink it — and Ron's grateful 'Thank you' — is a quick character beat that rewards familiarity with Ron's relationship with Scotch.

jokes.text: Tom's post-ceremony lament: 'Just this once, I thought I nailed something.' April: 'You worked hard and you got really close.' Tom: 'Close only counts in horse grenades.'
jokes.setup: Tom is dejected that his officiant vision didn't fully come to pass
jokes.punchline: His mangled version of 'close only counts in horseshoes and hand grenades' combines them into the nonsense portmanteau 'horse grenades' — then confidently explains its etymology as being from 'the movie Seabiscuit'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Horse grenades' is a perfect malapropism that merges two idioms ('horseshoes' and 'hand grenades') into something that makes no sense but sounds confident. But the explanation makes it better: Tom not only defends the phrase but attributes it to 'the movie Seabiscuit' — a film about a horse, where grenades do not appear. The false confidence is immaculate. April's silent confusion and Tom's elaboration ('you can still blow the horse's legs off') compound the absurdism. The explanation actively makes the joke worse in a way that makes it funnier. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Tom's full explanation of 'horse grenades': 'if you're playing horseshoes, and then you throw a grenade at a horse, it doesn't have to be that close, and you can still blow the horse's legs off. It's from the movie Seabiscuit.'
jokes.setup: April questions 'What?' after 'horse grenades'
jokes.punchline: Tom elaborates with a fully developed scenario that mixes horseshoe games with anti-horse grenade violence, then incorrectly cites Seabiscuit
jokes.explanation: While id 63 captures the initial malapropism, the full explanation in id 64 is separately and perhaps even more hilarious. Tom has constructed a vivid, internally logical scenario where the phrase actually makes sense — you ARE playing horseshoes, you DO throw a grenade at a horse — and the logic is tight within its own absurd world. The Seabiscuit citation, placing this scenario in a children's horse movie, is the final touch. This could be scored as part of the same joke as id 63, but the escalation of the explanation merits its own entry. This is among the highest-craft jokes of the episode.

jokes.text: April's talking head: 'Chris can be very... Paternal.' — delivered with her signature reluctant admiration
jokes.setup: We see Chris giving Andy an earnest inspirational speech
jokes.punchline: April's confessional acknowledges it with a word ('paternal') that sounds like a critique but is actually a compliment, delivered as if she's mildly disgusted by her own observation
jokes.explanation: A small, well-observed talking-head beat. April saying something faintly complimentary about someone (Chris) while clearly resistant to doing so is a recurring character note executed well. The pause before 'Paternal.' is the joke — she had to find the most clinical word possible.

jokes.text: Leslie's final talking head: 'When you're in love, everything seems like a sign.' / 'I love my husband. I love my job. And I love my friends. Even though they really can't handle their booze.'
jokes.setup: Leslie gives an emotional closing confessional about the night
jokes.punchline: After a series of sincere declarations of love, she adds the qualification that her friends 'really can't handle their booze' — an affectionate but pointed observation
jokes.explanation: A classic sitcom comedic closer — emotional declaration undercut by a specific, real observation. 'They really can't handle their booze' is the right button: loving but slightly exasperated. Good economy in the overall structure of the confessional.

jokes.text: Leslie's talking head closer: 'I love my husband. I love my job. And I love my friends. Even though they really can't handle their booze.'
jokes.setup: Leslie delivers an emotional summation of the night
jokes.punchline: The warm declaration of love ends with a mildly disappointed assessment of her friends' alcohol tolerance
jokes.explanation: A good button for a confessional. The pivot from genuine sentiment to mild complaint is a classic Parks structure. 'Really can't handle their booze' as the final note on a wedding episode is warm and funny.

jokes.text: The visual gag of drunk/celebrating friends visible in the background as Leslie and Ben try to sneak away: 'Hey, we should just go, right? Careful.'
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben want to leave their own impromptu wedding reception
jokes.punchline: The 'Careful.' implies the friends are in a chaotic enough state that the newlyweds must navigate carefully past them
jokes.explanation: A mild visual beat — the callback to Leslie's observation about her friends' drinking is confirmed here. More of a scene-transition joke than a standalone laugh. Functional.

jokes.text: Ron's talking head about making the wedding rings by forging metal in a cast-iron waffle maker with an acetylene torch and antifreeze — 'Any moron with a crucible, an acetylene torch, and a cast-iron waffle maker could have done the same.' / 'People who buy things are suckers.'
jokes.setup: The episode reveals how Ron solved the ring problem — by fabricating the rings himself from scratch
jokes.punchline: Ron's process is elaborate, expert, and genuinely impressive (smelting, casting, tempering, forging). His dismissal: 'Any moron could have done the same.' His philosophical conclusion: 'People who buy things are suckers.'
jokes.explanation: A perfect Ron Swanson closing statement that earns its position as the episode's final joke. The reveal that Ron solved the ring problem by smelting metal in a waffle maker with an acetylene torch is extraordinary — and then dismissing it as something 'any moron' could do is perfectly Ron. The coda — 'People who buy things are suckers' — is a complete encapsulation of Ron's philosophy delivered as the episode's last word. The character integration is perfect: this joke could not exist for any other character in television. Earns 8+.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben are getting married, and have to cram months of planning into two hours. Meanwhile, Ron's temper gets him in trouble.
insight: Romantic milestone trades laughs for warmth—62 jokes land softer than usual Parks fare.
